title: Don Jr.’s Wedding Trap
excerpt: I f you were a Russian intelligence operative trying to penetrate the American president’s inner circle, you could hardly have done much better than Umar Kremle
body: I f you were a Russian intelligence operative trying to penetrate the American president’s inner circle, you could hardly have done much better than Umar Kremlev did last May
Kremlev, a boxing promoter from outside Moscow, rented a private island in the Bahamas for Donald Trump Jr. to host his uber-luxe wedding celebration

Four of President Trump’s children, along with their spouses, were sequestered with Kremlev and a gaggle of other Russians during a party that went on for three days, according to an investigation by ProPublica published last week

The guest list of family and close friends included the president’s two sons-in-law: Jared Kushner, one of his key interlocutors with Moscow, and Michael Boulos, whose father is a senior adviser to Trump on Arab and Middle Eastern Affairs

A VIP party like that is what spies call a target-rich environment. “It’s an intelligence service’s dream to have so much time with these people, when alcohol is flowing and people’s guards are down,” Marc Polymeropoulos, who used to oversee the CIA’s clandestine operations in Russia, told me

When foreign agents gain access to such a setting, he said, “they are building relationships, gaining assessment data on targets, and perhaps even setting future contact, all precisely part of the recruitment cycle.” Kremlev shelled out for one night on a private island, as well as a fireworks display, which together can cost upwards of $170,000—a pittance, given the potential payoff

The president, who didn’t attend the wedding, defended the gift, claiming that he, too, had thrown wedding parties for people. “With all of that being said, I understand that Don’s paid him back,” Trump told reporters on Friday, although he didn’t say how much money his son planned to reimburse the Russian
The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Robert Garcia of California, has started an investigation
And yesterday, a Republican senator, John Curtis of Utah, called on his colleagues to investigate the wedding reception and issue a subpoena for Trump Jr
Kremlev, who did not respond to a request for comment, has been sanctioned by Ukraine but not by the United States
He owes his position, and apparently his wealth, to Russian President Vladimir Putin

Current and former intelligence officials in the U.S. and Europe who have spent their career working against Russia told me that his gift to Trump’s son should be viewed as the continuation of a long-standing state effort to influence and potentially compromise people in the president’s orbit
Kremlev, born Umar Lutfulloyev, grew up in a suburb of Moscow and has family roots in Tajikistan
After a few criminal convictions for extortion and battery in the early 2000s, he got into the boxing business

At age 28, Lutfulloyev changed his name to Kremlev, which essentially translates to “the Kremlin’s man.” Around this time, he joined the Night Wolves —ostensibly a patriotic biker gang but really more of a paramilitary and propaganda arm for Putin
The Russian president has previously mounted a bike and joined the gang on rides in the Crimean peninsula, an occupied territory of Ukraine
In 2014, following Russia’s first invasion of Ukraine, the U.S
Treasury Department sanctioned the Night Wolves, whose members allegedly “conducted intimidation and criminal activities” in the country
It was in the Night Wolves that Kremlev met Alexey Rubezhnoy, a former member of the FSB, Russia’s main security agency
Rubezhnoy is the current head of the Presidential Security Service, in charge of physical protection for the famously paranoid Russian president

According to Proekt , an independent Russian media outlet that specializes in investigative reporting, Rubezhnoy put Kremlev in position to take over the International Boxing Association, which now serves as an instrument of Russian soft power and a focal point for the Russian government’s rhetorical attacks on LGBTQ people and transgender athletes
Rubenzhnoy also lobbied Putin to nationalize a chain of car dealerships and for Kremlev to lead the company, Proekt reported

The 43-year-old Kremlev is frequently described in the press as an oligarch, a broadly applied term that, if it means anything these days, describes someone who owes his fortunes to the leader of Russia
Kremlev is just the kind of person the CIA would want to recruit because of his proximity to Putin and Russian state leadership

Yet there he was, ingratiating himself with Trump’s eldest son, who is also a close ally of Vice President Vance and one of the most influential figures on the American political right. “Espionage is a people business, and access is its holy grail,” John Sipher, a former CIA officer who worked in Moscow and spent his career focused on Russia, told me
Trump Jr.’s Russian guests, he said, had “myriad opportunities for cultivation and exploitation

A shared contact, stray comment, or a business proposition or follow-up meeting can provide information and access that may be leveraged in countless ways.” From the point of view of the U.S. government, which tries to prevent compromising encounters with politically influential Americans, “this is the stuff of counterintelligence nightmares,” Sipher said
K remlev’s past and his current connections are well known to the U.S. government and its partners
The Ukrainian government has sanctioned him, citing his close relationship with Putin, Rubezhnoy, and Russian security agencies

Kremlev is also heavily involved with Healthy Fatherland, an organization run by his wife’s twin sister, which Ukraine has sanctioned for its alleged role in the kidnapping and “rehabilitation” of Ukrainian children
A Ukrainian intelligence official told me that its domestic security agency has a thick file on Kremlev
In 2021, for reasons that remain unexplained, U.S

Customs and Border Protection denied a waiver for Kremlev to enter the United States. [ Read: Ukraine’s short-lived comeback ] Before Kremlev took over the boxing association, it was run by Gafur Rakhimov, an Uzbek businessman whom the Treasury Department publicly identified as an organized crime figure in 2012 because of his alleged membership in Brother’s Circle, a Russian criminal network involved in international heroin trafficking

Treasury sanctioned him again five years later for providing material support to another notorious group, Thieves in Law, which originated in Stalinist prison camps in the Soviet Union and is akin to the Italian Cosa Nostra
Rakhimov’s career is a manifestation of the blurry lines in Russia between organized crime, international sports, and the state security apparatus

The U.S. designations, as well as concerns about the International Boxing Association’s ties to the Russian banking system, prompted the International Olympic Committee to block the association from organizing the sport at the 2020 Tokyo Games
In 2023, USA Boxing withdrew from the IBA, which Kremlev now ran, citing his governmental ties as well as the association’s financial dependency on sanctioned companies
Gazprom, a Russian state-owned energy corporation, had been its largest sponsor
What Trump Jr. knew about Kremlev’s history is still unknown

When reporters pressed his father, the president suggested that his son “didn’t do a background check.” Within the West Wing, another tough headline elicited some groans and eye rolls, as well as quiet acknowledgment that the ProPublica report would, yet again, spark questions about the relationship between Russia and the Trumps

title: David Ellison Will Get Control of CNN After All
excerpt: Eighteen months ago, David Ellison was mostly known as an ATM for Hollywood producers seeking to pad out budgets for dad-core flicks such as Jack Ryan: Shadow R
body: Eighteen months ago, David Ellison was mostly known as an ATM for Hollywood producers seeking to pad out budgets for dad-core flicks such as Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit , Jack Reacher: Never Go Back , and Transformers: Rise of the Beasts
But now, thanks to a timely reallocation of his father’s money , he’s set to be one of the biggest news-media moguls in American history
Having already taken control of CBS News—with little to show for it audience-wise but plenty ideologically —he seems clear to add CNN to his roster of outlets
His acquisition , through Paramount, of Warner Bros
Discovery has been held up by a lawsuit filed by blue-state attorneys general over antitrust questions
One reported goal of the AGs was to have Ellison sell CNN in order to close the deal, though California’s Rob Bonta labeled that speculation
But yesterday morning, those AGs appeared to give up their fight

As Benjamin Mullin, David McCabe, Shawn Hubler, and Laurel Rosenhall at The New York Times reported: After weeks of on-again-off-again negotiations, Paramount and the states agreed to a number of concessions to complete the deal, according to the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss details not yet made public
The entertainment giant has agreed to establish a board of journalists to ensure the editorial independence of CNN and CBS News and committed to distributing 30 movies in theaters every year
The company also pledged to spend an additional $1.5 billion on film production over the next five years

So although another major national news outlet will be under the control of a major Trump ally, at least there’ll be “a board of journalists to ensure the editorial independence”! (That this is happening while the president Ellison supports is banning all CNN reporters from the White House adds a tragicomic veneer to the story.) If this particular move sounds familiar, that’s because such “boards” have been a part of other news-company acquisitions that have raised similar concerns about antitrust or editorial control
These boards’ effectiveness has been, to be generous, extremely limited

Two of the most prominent examples—both involving Rupert Murdoch—offer little reason for optimism. [ From the April 2025 issue: Growing up Murdoch ] The first began in 1981, when Murdoch wanted to purchase The Times of London and The Sunday Times
The editors of both papers were skeptical

In order to avoid an inquiry by Britain’s antitrust authority, Murdoch agreed to empower a set of “independent national directors” who would have to sign off on the firing or hiring of any top editor, and who would also resolve any major disputes between Murdoch and editors

As the legendary editor Harold Evans put it in his 1983 book, Good Times, Bad Times : [Murdoch had] guaranteed that the editors would have control of the political policy of their newspapers; that they would have freedom within fixed annual budgets; that the editors would not be subject to instruction from either the proprietor or management on the selection and balance of news and opinion; that instructions to journalists would be given only by their editor; and that any future sale of the titles would require the agreement of a majority of the independent national directors
In my year as editor of The Times, Murdoch broke all these guarantees

He put his point of view very simply to the home editor of The Times, Fred Emery, when he summoned him from holiday on 4 March to his office shortly before asking for my resignation: ‘I give instructions to my editors all round the world, why shouldn’t I in London?’ Evans lasted only a year under Murdoch’s ownership
A longer run was had by the conservative editor Andrew Neil, who edited The Sunday Times from 1983 to 1994

Giving parliamentary testimony in 2008 , Neil said that the “independence” offered by these outside board members was not about real authority; it was about smoothing the path of an important news outlet into regime-friendly hands: First of all, let us just remind ourselves
It was a conceit invented by John Biffen and the Thatcher Government to allow Mr
Murdoch to take over these papers in the first place, and it was put in place for that reason
It was not really put in place to protect the independence of the editors

Neil, arguably the most prominent conservative British journalist of the past half century, was no fellow traveler of the left-wing Guardian , yet he contrasted that paper’s control by the Scott Trust with the kabuki theater of an “independent board”: The Scott Trust is a perfectly legitimate way of running a newspaper and, as you can see from the success of The Guardian and its on-line success globally, it works
It is entirely different from the strong proprietor who controls the shares and the business of that company appointing a couple of trustees as a fig-leaf
The second example came in 2007, when Murdoch made an unsolicited offer to the Bancroft family to acquire Dow Jones and its flagship newspaper, The Wall Street Journal

Several family members were concerned about what Murdoch ownership might do to the newspaper’s quality, and as part of the eventual sale, Murdoch agreed to the appointment of a “Dow Jones Special Committee” that would, much like its London predecessor, have final say over the hiring and firing of top editors , as well as changes that could be construed as forcing an editor out

With that guarantee in place, enough hesitant Bancrofts were persuaded to sell—though not everyone was on board. “Although I’m convinced that News Corp. offer is very generous in financial terms,” Dieter von Holtzbrinck, a Dow Jones director, wrote in his resignation letter , “I’m very worried that Dow Jones unique journalistic values will long-term strongly suffer after the proposed sale.” He added, “I do not believe that the ‘Special Committee’ can finally prevent Mr
Murdoch from doing what he wants to do, from acting his way.” Barely four months after the transaction closed, he was proved right
Murdoch managed a nifty end run around the “special committee” and ousted the newsroom’s top editor , Marcus Brauchli

Instead, he layered over him, naming the former Times of London editor Robert Thomson as publisher, but giving him direct oversight of the newsroom rather than the position’s usual business-side responsibilities

Brauchli, frozen out of major decisions in the newsroom he allegedly led, sent a note to staff saying he had “come to believe the new owners should have a managing editor of their choosing.” Brauchli was well compensated with a nice “consulting” gig for Dow Jones
Because Brauchli had resigned rather than be fired, the approval of the special committee was not required

Murdoch informed its members as a fait accompli, telling one , “I have no doubt that The New York Times will make trouble with it for a day or two, but I’m not too bothered by it.” The committee later issued a statement in which members “expressed the view that learning of the Brauchli matter after the fact failed to meet the letter and the spirit of the agreement.” But alas, the committee “decided there was no practical way to ‘unresign’ Brauchli and start the process over.” [ David A

Graham: Hindsight is 2024 ] The reporter Sarah Ellison (no relation to David), in her book on the Murdoch takeover of the Journal , described the special committee as “an artificial set of rules he would inevitably circumvent,” which seems dead-on
Right now, we don’t know much about what a CNN (or CBS News) “independent editorial board” will look like

Bloomberg News reports that it “will be composed only of journalists, with no executives or shareholders allowed to join,” and that “the board will be required to have political balance.” The deal does not appear to have any sort of hard enforcement mechanism built in for any violations of the “the letter and the spirit” of the editorial independence agreement. (By contrast, it does include a $30 million penalty for each film Paramount promises to release to theaters but doesn’t.) But let’s be blunt
No matter how well intentioned the members of these committees may be, if David Ellison wants to get around them, he will
The rules being put in place are an artificial set that a billionaire owner will inevitably circumvent
Such “independent” boards are PR gestures , not vehicles for editorial protection

title: The ‘New Word’ Trump Hates
excerpt: Of all the outrages and betrayals that Donald Trump has had perpetrated against him—by ungrateful subordinates, by obstreperous prosecutors, by treacherous jour
body: Of all the outrages and betrayals that Donald Trump has had perpetrated against him—by ungrateful subordinates, by obstreperous prosecutors, by treacherous journalists—perhaps his saddest falling-out is with a simple word. “Starting on day one, we will defeat inflation quickly, and we will make America affordable again,” he declared in an ad during his 2024 presidential campaign
A year later, Trump confessed to still having some affinity for the word

Speaking at a summit hosted by McDonald’s, the president promised imminent prosperity: “That begins with making America, we have to do—the word is affordable —and affordable should be our word, not theirs.” These days, the word itself is, like all of Trump’s enemies, the frequent target of invective

The president describes the concept of affordability as, variously, a Democratic “ con job ,” as “a new word—nobody ever heard the word,” and, most damningly of all, as “ fake .” The reasons for this lexical animosity are clear
The word that the president once wielded with great effect against Democrats in 2024 is now being used against him with seemingly equal effect by his opponents

Affordability is the Democrats’ unifying theme, which, despite them lacking coherence on almost every other issue, may be enough to carry them to victory in the November midterm elections. (Nate Silver estimates that in the generic congressional ballot, Democrats are leading by a crushing 7.5 percentage points.) And no wonder

Inflation remains high; gas prices, which Trump promised in 2024 would settle below $2 a gallon, are now above $4 thanks to the president’s war with Iran; mortgage rates, which Trump said would drop to 2 percent, are instead near 7 percent. [ Marc Novicoff: Gas prices could cost Republicans the midterms ] But Democrats shouldn’t expect to hang on to their advantage here; far more likely, the inversion will recur

You can imagine America settling into a persistent politics of affordability, in which the arguments are always the same but the positions of accuser and accused are swapped depending on who holds power

Democrats are, for example, pledging that if they win the midterm elections, they will crusade for lower costs “of groceries, of housing, of childcare and elder care.” Perhaps such competition would be salutary; more likely, it would be Sisyphean—an unending cycle of accusation, disappointment, and recrimination
The first is that affordability politics are a breeding ground for economically illiterate policy ideas
Popular anger over inflation is usually directed at cumulative price increases over the course of years
But literally decreasing prices is exceptionally hard to accomplish, even if that is what voters want

In this heady environment, discredited ideas such as price controls and even the direct provision of goods—as New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is attempting with government-run grocery stores—make their resurgence

Affordability politics also encourages unvarnished attempts at bribing voters, as Trump attempted with his pledge to give $5,000 to every American adult should Republicans keep control of Congress. (This is both a subpar reason to add another $1.3 trillion to America’s $40 trillion in national debt and a very good way to exacerbate inflation .) [ From the August 2026 issue: The ‘consumer socialism’ trap ] The second problem of affordability politics is what these proposed solutions do to what little remains of voter trust in government

Every election cycle, politicians make promises for widespread price relief, package them into neat advertisements, and relay these to voters a mind-numbing number of times, only for these promises to go undelivered—because they were unworkable from the start
This may not inspire apathy among voters so much as anger and irritability
It also encourages anti-incumbency of the kind that explains why Americans have, in every presidential election since 2016, opted for the challenging party’s candidate
The third problem is the cumulative cost of short-termist affordability politics
Neither party in this election cycle is making much reference to the national debt, even though the United States has surpassed, for the first time ever, $1 trillion in interest costs this year
Deficit spending shows no sign of slowing down, even though the American economy is not in recession and the country is only mildly at war
But there is no political incentive to suggest that such spending cannot persist
Instead, Democrats traditionally propose new social expenditures and subsidies, whereas Republicans propose general tax cuts

The new approach, favored by populists, is to offer both: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for the Senate race in Michigan, has pitched “a cost-of-living exemption on federal taxes up to $50,000” while also establishing Medicare for All and universal child care—to be paid for by the rich
Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee for the Senate race in Iowa, is pitching more government support for house purchases, child care, and rural hospitals while cutting taxes
Why begrudge the entire enterprise of affordability politicking? Isn’t the job of elected officials ostensibly to improve the lives of their constituents? Yes, indeed

And it is of course still possible to durably decrease prices with good governmental policy: You can, for example, slowly reduce the cost of housing by reducing restrictions on building, or reduce health costs by expanding the supply of doctors
This requires some forbearance and sophistication on the part of the politician—and, unfortunately, both qualities are negatively selected against in the current political-attention economy
It is better to make headlines with snappier pledges to freeze the rent or nationalize the health system
You can safely assume that at the conclusion of the midterms, the 2028 presidential election will begin in earnest and affordability will be one of its bywords
You can also dread the litany of bad ideas it will spawn.

title: America’s Biggest Dating Company Is Betting on Trad Values
excerpt: If a dating app existed in the 1950s, you might expect it to look like Upward
body: If a dating app existed in the 1950s, you might expect it to look like Upward
On “chivalry mode,” users can establish that the man in a straight pairing will message the woman first
With “marriage timeline,” they can specify how soon they’d like to marry

In one promotional image, a man leans against a car; below him is the caption “Known to change a tire, not his feelings for you.” In another, a man smiles, coffee cup in hand: “Known to cover the reservation and the check.” A woman in a cowboy hat is “often described as wifey material.” This is not, in fact, a glitch in the time-space continuum, the 20th century folding in on the 21st
It’s the newest big project for Match Group, the company that owns an abundance of dating apps, including Hinge and Tinder

Today, Match relaunched Upward, formerly a Christian dating app but now a home for anybody who wants to settle down—the old-fashioned way. “This is modern courtship in action,” the company’s press release reads. “Women are clear about their standards, men pursue with purpose, and both move toward marriage together.” [ Read: The great romance slump ] Any number of other platforms let you date with the purpose of getting hitched, of course
On Hinge or Tinder or Bumble, you can indicate what type of relationship you’re looking for and whether you want children
I see plenty of people on dating apps openly calling for a soulmate, a spouse, a co-parent—and I’m in New York City, not Tuscaloosa
What Match is capitalizing on, though, isn’t simply a yearning for matrimony or parenthood

It’s leveraging what’s arguably a regressive streak in the culture: a tendency to romanticize the scripts that more Americans used to follow, which told them how men and women should behave and what they should value
Internally, Match calls Upward’s audience the “next-gen traditionalists.” Now the company is betting on them
About 10 months ago, Match pulled together some data on its apps’ audiences
The one that stood out, surprisingly, was Upward
The singles using Upward, though they sometimes talked about faith, didn’t overall seem keen to discuss the details of their religious practice
Profile prompts such as “What’s your favorite Bible verse?” weren’t widely used
Match’s chief marketing officer, Stephanie Danzi, told me that instead, the unifying factor appeared to be a specific vision of the future
These people wanted to get married and have kids—not probably or eventually, but seriously and soon
When Match surveyed couples who had met on Upward, they found that the average time from match to marriage was less than a year
Upward, in other words, looked like an opportunity
Marriage rates have been falling for years, but that doesn’t mean people aren’t hoping to tie the knot
In the Kinsey Institute’s recent 2026 “Singles in America” study , funded by Match, 72 percent of Gen Z participants—more than any other generation—said they want to get married

I’ve seen this in my own reporting: For plenty of people, marriage seems like both a far-off goal and an essential one. [ Read: The unglamorous truth about the average tradwife ] Desiring marriage doesn’t necessarily mean you want to follow strict gender norms
But young people today are veering toward traditionalism; tradwife influencers and manosphere podcasters aren’t the only ones who think that men and women ought to stay in separate lanes
In a global Ipsos poll from last year, about a third of Gen Z men agreed that “a wife should always obey her husband”—more than double the share of Baby Boomer men who said the same
Although only 6 percent of Baby Boomer women affirmed the statement, nearly 20 percent of Gen Z women did

And in that “Singles in America” survey, more than half of respondents—and 70 percent of Gen Z men—said that women should be their children’s primary caregiver, up from 34 percent of respondents in 2013

In promo videos, a couple who met on the app practices “chivalrymaxxing”: the husband opens a car door for his wife, gives her his jacket, picks her up, and carries her around. (In an especially unsubtle bit of conservative coding, Match mentions that the couple’s first date involved Chick-fil-A.) The press release announcing the relaunch notes that the app’s new design draws from “Americana” and that the tone is “nostalgic.” A quintessential Upward member, Danzi said, might be a young woman looking for a “ring by spring”: She hopes to be engaged by the time she graduates
I thought of the 2003 movie Mona Lisa Smile , which is set in the 1950s
Julia Roberts plays a Wellesley art-history professor who tries to show her students that they can pursue dreams other than marriage
When I watched that as a girl, the idea that women would need this kind of convincing seemed disturbing but blessedly buried in history
Danzi didn’t describe Upward as an anti-feminist app—far from it
She explained that many Zoomers find romance confusing and intimidating; sometimes, they know what they want but not how to convey it

With Upward, “the rules of courtship are really clear; the end goal is really clear,” she said. “So you don’t have to deal with the ambiguity of like, I don’t want to come on too strong by saying I want to have four kids or whatever it may be.” And if women say they want to be pursued, if they want to be homemakers, if they want a ring by spring—well, Match is helping them achieve their goals

Upward, Danzi said, is giving people “the agency to go after what’s really important to them.” [ Read: Bumble hands the first move back to men ] Match isn’t the only dating titan to make this argument
The app Bumble, when it launched in 2014, branded itself as a feminist app with the premise that the woman messages the man first

But then the company announced last month that many women no longer want the duty of initiating; men are now allowed to start the conversation. “You have to move with culture, or you get left behind,” the platform’s founder, Whitney Wolfe Herd, said at The Atlantic Festival last week. “You have to listen to data.” Bumble read the winds—and the winds, apparently, were trad
Modern dating can be complicated in some ways it didn’t used to be
Women have to decide what they want to do with the agency that comes from greater financial power
Men have to consider what they’ll bring to a relationship besides just money in the bank
The cost of choice is responsibility: to comprehend your own complex desires and also to communicate them, which, as Danzi noted, many young adults struggle with

title: The ICE Officer in Austin Wasn’t Wearing a Body Cam
excerpt: Sign up for Inside the Trump Presidency , a newsletter featuring coverage of the second Trump term
body: Sign up for Inside the Trump Presidency , a newsletter featuring coverage of the second Trump term

T he ICE officer who shot a Venezuelan man last weekend in Austin was a recent hire who was not wearing his body camera, three officials at the Department of Homeland Security with knowledge of the incident told me

The officer, who has not been publicly identified, was hired last year, according to two of the officials, but he previously worked for another federal law-enforcement agency, one of the officials said
The officials were not authorized to discuss the investigation into the shooting, which left Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez with a bullet lodged in his upper torso, according to his attorney
ICE officials have rushed to distribute body-worn cameras to officers since the fatal shootings in July of a Mexican construction contractor in Texas and a Colombian delivery driver in Maine
Officers making arrests are required to have the cameras at all times

The agency has directed officers to activate the devices prior to engaging in enforcement activity, the three officials said, and ICE instructs them to stop recording only when the incident has safely concluded
Officers who do not follow these instructions are required to submit a written statement to their supervisors and could face possible disciplinary action, the three officials said
DHS and ICE public-affairs officials did not immediately respond to questions about the incident in Austin and whether the officer will face consequences
On Sunday, the officer was working with a partner who was driving in a separate vehicle
That second officer had a body-worn camera that was turned on, two officials told me
The officers were checking license plates using a system that helps them find targets for arrest using commercial databases and federal immigration files
When they ran the plates from the blue Toyota Corolla driven by Garcés Pérez, the officers saw he had an outstanding deportation order from an immigration judge
The ICE officers, who were driving unmarked vehicles, attempted to pull Garcés Pérez over, but he drove away, nearly striking one of the officers, according to one of the DHS officials
The official said the incident was recorded by the body camera of the ICE officer’s partner
The officers followed Garcés Pérez in their vehicles
The officer without the body camera found Garcés Pérez and attempted to detain him
When Garcés Pérez attempted to drive away again, that officer pulled his gun and fired, striking Garcés Pérez in the back, both of the officials told me

A bystander video recorded just after the shooting shows an officer wearing a cap and a face covering standing next to the Corolla speaking with Garcés Pérez, who clutches at the wound on his back and winces in pain. [ Read: ICE has quietly changed its deadly-force rule ] G arcés Pérez, 28, briefly received medical treatment for the gunshot wound, then was taken to an ICE detention center southwest of Austin

As his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, gathered with supporters and journalists at a news conference yesterday, Garcés Pérez addressed the crowd by phone and with the help of a translator. “I have not received the medical attention that I require,” Garcés Pérez said
Lincoln-Goldfinch said that Garcés Pérez was taken out of the hospital after just four hours and then had to sleep on the floor of the detention center
She said he was moved to a hospital after reporting “left-side paralysis” and severe pain. “He should have stayed in the hospital all of this time,” she told CNN
Representative Joaquin Castro of Texas, a Democrat, said this morning that Garcés Pérez had been transferred back to the ICE detention center
Lincoln-Goldfinch said her client has a valid driver’s license and was making deliveries for DoorDash when ICE attempted to stop him and rammed his car

She said Garcés Pérez entered the United States legally in 2024 through the CBP One program, which allowed asylum seekers to enter the country and pursue asylum claims through a “parole” program offered by the Biden administration
President Trump canceled that program, so if Garcés Pérez did not obtain another form of legal-immigration status, he would be potentially subject to ICE arrest

Lincoln-Goldfinch said her client was issued a deportation order because his court documents were sent to the wrong address. “I see this all the time in my practice and it’s a mistake we can easily correct
It does not justify shooting people in the street,” Lincoln-Goldfinch wrote in a social-media post
The Trump administration launched a hiring spree at ICE last year to add 10,000 deportation officers and more than double the number of personnel deployed on U.S. streets
The officer who fatally shot the Colombian immigrant Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine was also a new hire

Veteran officers at ICE have repeatedly shared their concerns with me about the qualifications and competence of new recruits, especially those sent through a fast-track training course in which classroom hours were cut by more than half

ICE has ended the fast-track program for new hires, but one senior ICE official told me that a large number of the officers the agency recruited have since been disqualified or let go. [ Read: The education of Markwayne Mullin ] ICE arrests increased this summer to 50,000 a month, the highest levels ever recorded by the agency, which remains under intense White House pressure to carry out 1 million deportations a year
After Durán Guerrero’s killing, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin ordered a pause on most vehicle stops by ICE officers, citing the need to finish distributing body cameras and improve officer training
But Trump reversed that order a day later, after immigration-enforcement hard-liners protested
ICE training instructs officers that the use of deadly force against a fleeing suspect is not permissible unless there is an imminent risk of harm to law-enforcement personnel or the public
DHS’s inspector general is investigating the fatal shooting of Durán Guerrero in Maine as well as the killing of 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston on July 7
The findings from those investigations have not been released.

title: The Download: why AI’s latest breakthroughs and fears may be more hype than reality
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
Don’t be fooled by this summer of AI hype  —Timnit Gebru, executive director of the Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR), and Emily M

Bender, professor of linguistics at the University of Washington It’s been a busy few months for AI hype, with companies making breathless claims about hacking, mathematical breakthroughs, and the prospect of self-improving superintelligence
In all these cases, massive fanfare from the companies, presented as mea culpas in the hacking incidents, has been accompanied by intense press coverage
But once experts have had time to examine what happened, very different stories emerge
There’s a strong commercial incentive to overstate AI capabilities
The authors argue that the illusion of speed and urgency promulgated by the tech companies is also a ploy to misdirect policymakers and the public
Here’s why they say we must remain skeptical about AI hype

title: Don’t be fooled by this summer of AI hype
excerpt: At the end of April, Anthropic claimed that its model Claude Mythos is better at finding software vulnerabilities than most security experts
body: At the end of April, Anthropic claimed that its model Claude Mythos is better at finding software vulnerabilities than most security experts
Then we had the OpenAI–Hugging Face hacking incident , after which Anthropic (proudly) and Meta (reluctantly) disclosed similar incidents involving their models
This was followed by Anthropic ’s claim that one of its models had made a mathematical breakthrough; soon OpenAI claimed a mathematical breakthrough of its own

Most recently, Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon went viral announcing his departure from the company, claiming that it and OpenAI are “racing straight towards self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Each of these events was mostly covered breathlessly by the press, often repeating the companies’ anthropomorphizing framings —which are designed to portray their software is not only powerful but incipient “ artificial general intelligence .” So what is really going on? Are we witnessing a massive, civilization-changing set of technological breakthroughs, or is this marketing? In all these incidents, massive fanfare from the companies (presented as mea culpas in illicit hacking cases) is accompanied by intense press coverage
Once there is time for experts in the relevant fields to examine what happened, a very different story emerges, but one that gets less media attention

Regarding the “hacking” incidents, cybersecurity experts say the story is more about OpenAI’s negligence and failure to adopt basic, established security practices than about “models gone rogue” or “AI agents creating civilizations.”  As for the mathematical results, mathematicians who were initially “stunned” by OpenAI’s press release saying that its latest chatbot, Astra, solved problems that “have been open and seen no progress on the main result for at least a decade”—but they later realized that the results weren’t as “novel as first appeared.” Since then, mathematicians have accused the company of research misconduct and plagiarism, and they’ve reiterated that Astra didn’t make a “profound intellectual leap.” Just weeks later, OpenAI claimed its own mathematical breakthrough

Two days before, Tristan Buckmaster, a math professor at New York University’s Courant Institute, published a bombshell statement suggesting that OpenAI had stolen other people’s work and improperly attributed it.  Claims of incipient, dangerous superintelligence are not based in good scientific or engineering practice
Rather, they are narratives based in ideologies of transhumanism, eugenics, and wishful thinking about imagined future digital humans
It’s worth thinking about why there is so much attention on computer programming and math as fields in which to apply large language models and related technology
Not only are they often elevated as the pinnacle of human intellectual achievement, but they involve problems where answers, once suggested, can be verified
The former property helps AI hype mongers sell the idea that they are building everything machines

The latter makes math and coding problems easier to tune systems for, since system output (sequences of likely words or pieces of computer code) can be evaluated without having to pay data workers to look at and annotate each one
Mathematicians in particular have warned against corporations using their field in this way

A statement signed by hundreds of them says there is “currently a strong commercial incentive on the part of the technology industry to overstate the capabilities of their products” and asks policymakers to “consult with experts, including mathematicians, in forming policy decisions rather than relying on press releases or popular reporting of mathematical results.” We echo this call and note that the illusion of speed and urgency promulgated by the tech companies is also a ploy to misdirect both policymakers and the public

Unfortunately, it sometimes works, such as with Senator Bernie Sanders’s well-meaning but ultimately misguided proposed legislation to prevent the development of “artificial superintelligence.” Describing them as “superintelligence” or “rogue models” ascribes agency to products rather than to the companies building them

This framing markets these companies’ products as “superhuman” and, at the same time, helps the companies evade accountability for their actions.  Instead of OpenAI being prosecuted for creating malware that hacked another company, press releases, news outlets, media personalities, and lawmakers refer to “rogue models” as if they acted on their own

Instead of researchers being questioned about their companies’ habit of plagiarizing academics’ work or using customer data to train models without consent, the public’s imagination is redirected to fears about what the future might hold upon the arrival of fictional superintelligent machines.   The AI industry has even suggested that popular, bipartisan anti-data-center activism is a “distraction” from attempts to regulate the impending, scary, “superhuman” machines these companies are building

According to the AI industry, we should be more worried about a fictional machine god than about the climate catastrophe that these data centers exacerbate, the asthma suffered by those living near them, the rising electricity bills of the public subsidizing them, or the water that is redirected to cooling them .  We know better than to make decisions based on marketing and better than to capitulate to corporate pressure to make those decisions quickly
Wise decision-making, by policymakers and communities, demands time to hear from independent experts and contextualize corporate claims

The best possible outcome from this summer of hype is that policymakers and the public at large learn to take a breath, hold onto our skepticism, and recognize this kind of hype for what it is the next time it comes around

Timnit Gebru is executive director of DAIR and author of the forthcoming book Deep Unlearning: The Radicalization of a Tech Idealist , which is available for preorders now and set to publish on February 16
Bender is professor of linguistics at the University of Washington and coauthor of The AI Con .

title: Russia-Ukraine war is accelerating the dangerous race toward fully autonomous drones
url:
<title>Russia-Ukraine war is accelerating the dangerous race toward fully autonomous drones</title>
    <content type="html"><p>A battlefield dominated by fully autonomous drones capable of selecting and engaging targets <a href="https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodd/300009p.PDF">without human intervention</a> sounds like a dystopian sci-fi plot. And while that scenario has not yet arrived, the <a href="https://theconversation.com/topics/ukraine-invasion-2022-117045">conflict between Russia and Ukraine</a> has moved modern warfare a notch down that road.</p>

<p>In recent years, both nations have deployed semi-autonomous drones in combat and are rapidly <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/14/attacks-will-be-fully-autonomous-russia-ukraine-race-towards-ai-warfare">racing toward fully autonomous</a> unmanned aerial vehicles.</p>

<p>Given these developments and the pace of Russian and Ukrainian drone production, a battlefield with hundreds to thousands of fully autonomous drones operating is plausible within the next few years. Yet, the technology underpinning autonomous warfare risks outpacing the Russian and Ukrainian frameworks for maintaining some degree of human control over weapons. </p>

<p>As an <a href="https://keough.nd.edu/about/faculty-staff-directory/amy-mcauliffe/">expert on weapons technology</a>, I worry that the battlefield incentives to deploy more autonomous drones will completely push aside human targeting decisions related to using proportional force, avoiding strikes on non-combatants and limiting collateral damage.</p>

<h2>The creeping drone war</h2>

<p>Both Ukraine and Russia have increasingly prioritized the use and production of drones since the war began in February 2022. Unable to produce large numbers of one-way attack drones at first, Russia <a href="https://theconversation.com/russias-drone-pipeline-how-iran-helps-moscow-produce-an-ever-evolving-unmanned-fleet-272016">turned to Tehran</a> for technological assistance – and has steadily developed its own capacity. Ukraine had a nascent drone industry and has grown it using private defense firms and technological innovation.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Smoke bellows from a building" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761237/original/file-20260921-50-ttd7ur.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761237/original/file-20260921-50-ttd7ur.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761237/original/file-20260921-50-ttd7ur.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761237/original/file-20260921-50-ttd7ur.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761237/original/file-20260921-50-ttd7ur.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761237/original/file-20260921-50-ttd7ur.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761237/original/file-20260921-50-ttd7ur.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Flames engulf a building in Dnipro, Ukraine, hit by a Russian drone on Sept. 19, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/flames-engulf-a-store-building-hit-by-a-russian-drone-on-news-photo/2296389500?adppopup=true">Danyil Nikolaenko/Suspilne Ukraine/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>As the war has progressed, both sides have added autonomous features to existing drones, as well as developed new drones with autonomous capabilities. Specifically, both Russia and Ukraine have deployed drones with autonomous functions using AI on the battlefield to recognize targets, navigate and self-guide to targets.</p>

<p>In November 2025, a <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/ukrainian-drone-pilots-look-ai-battlefield-edge-2025-11-29/">Ukrainian first-person-view drone</a> used an AI-assisted guidance system to strike a probable Russian tank after the drone’s communications link with its operator was disrupted. A human operator selected the target, but the drone itself guided the final stages of the attack.</p>

<p>Reliable estimates of the numbers of these drones on the battlefield are unavailable. However, reports on their usage suggest they represent only a small percentage of the millions of drones both sides have deployed to date.</p>

<p>At the advanced end of the spectrum, Russia reportedly fielded at least one model of a <a href="https://www.longwarjournal.org/archives/2025/06/ukrainian-intelligence-details-russias-new-v2u-autonomous-loitering-munition.php">fully autonomous unmanned aerial vehicle</a> in early 2025. Ukrainian analysis of recovered Russian V2U drones revealed a small Nvidia computer designed to run AI-enabled decision-making software. Variants recovered in late 2025 no longer contained the external communications systems suggestive of operator control. </p>

<h2>Autonomous targeting</h2>

<p>The V2U’s technical systems are configured to enable autonomous selection and engagement of targets without operator intervention following launch.</p>

<p>Human operators have generally selected intended targets or target areas for moral reasons, highlighting the significance of the V2U’s ability to carry out these missions autonomously.</p>

<p><a href="https://csis-website-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-04/260413_Bondar_Russia_Drone.pdf?VersionId=po8ciEm5hTl_KvzVNc_OexC2X73N4Yol">The onboard AI</a> utilizes computer vision, allowing the drone to analyze images from its onboard sensors. It can autonomously recognize objects, track them, navigate and select potential targets. </p>

<p>In July, Russia employed a different AI-enabled drone in combat that demonstrated a less comprehensive form of autonomous targeting. The strike, on a gas station in Zaporizhzhia, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/24/world/europe/russia-drones-autonomous-ai-kill-ukraine-war.html?searchResultPosition=6">killed three Ukrainian civilians</a>. Human operators selected the gas station as the target area, while onboard software independently picked the final aim point.</p>

<p>Russia is also integrating versions of a similar technology into its Geran series unmanned aerial vehicles, which are based on Iran’s delta-wing Shaheed-136 attack drone. Some Gerans include a <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/vikrammittal/2026/08/09/russias-upgraded-geran-drones-are-targeting-ukraines-black-sea-ports/">seeker guidance package</a> that allows the onboard computer to guide the drone in the final flight phase, after a human operator initially selects the target. </p>

<p>Ukraine, for its part, has focused on <a href="https://www.csis.org/analysis/ukraines-future-vision-and-current-capabilities-waging-ai-enabled-autonomous-warfare">modular AI-driven packages</a>, including chips with embedded software and sometimes cameras, that it can install widely across drone and other platforms. It has fielded drones that use onboard AI to <a href="https://epravda.com.ua/tehnologiji/ukrajina-vpershe-zastosuvala-dron-nosiy-z-shi-807323/">identify targets</a> and guide them in their final flight phase. </p>

<p>One such module <a href="https://thefourthlaw.ai">tracks targets and guides the drone</a> the final 500 meters to them. The company that makes the computer advertises more advanced modules, which it claims will provide additional and even full autonomy. </p>

<p>Ukraine claims to have used more advanced autonomous drones on the battlefield as well. Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said in July that Ukraine used a drone that autonomously chooses targets with no radio connection to a human pilot in <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/31/world/europe/federov-ukraine-killer-robots.html">strikes in Russian-occupied Crimea</a> at an unspecified date. He added that Ukraine has not mass-produced this drone. </p>

<p>Ukraine also reportedly employed what have been dubbed <a href="https://united24media.com/war-in-ukraine/should-ukraine-have-to-justify-its-use-of-battlefield-ai-21775">fully autonomous</a> quadcopter drones two years ago against Russian forces near Bakhmut, Ukraine, <a href="https://smallwarsjournal.com/2026/08/17/fully-autonomous-drones-reportedly-kill-in-ukraine/">killing Russian soldiers</a>. However, reports that the drones were preprogrammed raise questions about whether the drones independently selected the targets.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A woman looks out a window at smoke billowing from a building in the distance." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761239/original/file-20260921-50-azcojo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761239/original/file-20260921-50-azcojo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761239/original/file-20260921-50-azcojo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761239/original/file-20260921-50-azcojo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761239/original/file-20260921-50-azcojo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=565&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761239/original/file-20260921-50-azcojo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=565&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761239/original/file-20260921-50-azcojo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=565&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Smoke rises from Russian oil producer Gazprom Neft’s Moscow oil refinery on Sept. 20, 2026, after a drone attack.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/woman-rides-in-a-bus-as-smoke-rises-from-the-area-of-the-news-photo/2295633995?adppopup=true">AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Battlefield advantages, ethical concerns</h2>

<p>Russian and Ukrainian drones with autonomous capabilities already have had battlefield impact, even though Kyiv and Moscow have not yet deployed the most advanced systems in large numbers. </p>

<p>The benefits of deployment are clear. Drones with autonomous functions reduce their dependence on communications links and can continue despite jamming and other forms of electronic warfare. These capabilities help enable strikes deep into each other’s territory. </p>

<p>Autonomous navigation and guidance in the final portion of flight can also improve drones’ ability to engage moving targets. Deployment of fully autonomous drones at scale could reduce the personnel required to operate large numbers.</p>

<p>But autonomous drones come with serious ethical concerns.</p>

<p>A major risk is that the development and employment of this technology leapfrogs the ability of Russia and Ukraine to maintain some type of human control over autonomous weapons. Ukrainian Ministry of Defense rules require keeping <a href="https://mod.gov.ua/en/explainers/what-is-the-kill-chain-and-how-does-ai-help-destroy-enemy-targets-faster">humans in the loop</a> for “combat” decisions, meaning that humans verify targets in the “<a href="https://united24media.com/war-in-ukraine/should-ukraine-have-to-justify-its-use-of-battlefield-ai-21775">final stages of interception</a>.” </p>

<p>In contrast, Russia’s arms control positions provide insights into its views on human control. Russian officials highlight “<a href="https://docs-library.unoda.org/Convention_on_Certain_Conventional_Weapons_-Group_of_Governmental_Experts_on_Lethal_Autonomous_Weapons_Systems_(2024)/CCW-GGE.1-2024-WP.6_-_Chair's_summary.pdf">human control</a>,” with a focus on the ability to alter the system, deactivate it or provide limitations, such as on the types of targets that it can engage. But Moscow does not stress that a human has to be in the loop for verifying targets before they strike them.</p>

<p>As worrying as that sounds now, the next step in AI drone warfare is even more concerning: Swarming drones that can hunt in packs of a few to thousands and autonomously alter their behavior based on communicating with one another present a frightening challenge to maintaining human control.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290877/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

    <summary>Drones with autonomous functions reduce dependence on communications links and can escape attempts at jamming. But they come with huge ethical risks.</summary>

excerpt: A battlefield dominated by fully autonomous drones capable of selecting and engaging targets without human intervention sounds like a dystopian sci-fi plot
body: A battlefield dominated by fully autonomous drones capable of selecting and engaging targets without human intervention sounds like a dystopian sci-fi plot
And while that scenario has not yet arrived, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine has moved modern warfare a notch down that road
In recent years, both nations have deployed semi-autonomous drones in combat and are rapidly racing toward fully autonomous unmanned aerial vehicles
Given these developments and the pace of Russian and Ukrainian drone production, a battlefield with hundreds to thousands of fully autonomous drones operating is plausible within the next few years
Yet, the technology underpinning autonomous warfare risks outpacing the Russian and Ukrainian frameworks for maintaining some degree of human control over weapons

As an expert on weapons technology , I worry that the battlefield incentives to deploy more autonomous drones will completely push aside human targeting decisions related to using proportional force, avoiding strikes on non-combatants and limiting collateral damage
The creeping drone war Both Ukraine and Russia have increasingly prioritized the use and production of drones since the war began in February 2022
Unable to produce large numbers of one-way attack drones at first, Russia turned to Tehran for technological assistance – and has steadily developed its own capacity
Ukraine had a nascent drone industry and has grown it using private defense firms and technological innovation
Flames engulf a building in Dnipro, Ukraine, hit by a Russian drone on Sept. 19, 2026

Danyil Nikolaenko/Suspilne Ukraine/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images As the war has progressed, both sides have added autonomous features to existing drones, as well as developed new drones with autonomous capabilities
Specifically, both Russia and Ukraine have deployed drones with autonomous functions using AI on the battlefield to recognize targets, navigate and self-guide to targets
In November 2025, a Ukrainian first-person-view drone used an AI-assisted guidance system to strike a probable Russian tank after the drone’s communications link with its operator was disrupted
A human operator selected the target, but the drone itself guided the final stages of the attack
Reliable estimates of the numbers of these drones on the battlefield are unavailable
However, reports on their usage suggest they represent only a small percentage of the millions of drones both sides have deployed to date
At the advanced end of the spectrum, Russia reportedly fielded at least one model of a fully autonomous unmanned aerial vehicle in early 2025
Ukrainian analysis of recovered Russian V2U drones revealed a small Nvidia computer designed to run AI-enabled decision-making software
Variants recovered in late 2025 no longer contained the external communications systems suggestive of operator control
Autonomous targeting The V2U’s technical systems are configured to enable autonomous selection and engagement of targets without operator intervention following launch
Human operators have generally selected intended targets or target areas for moral reasons, highlighting the significance of the V2U’s ability to carry out these missions autonomously
The onboard AI utilizes computer vision, allowing the drone to analyze images from its onboard sensors
It can autonomously recognize objects, track them, navigate and select potential targets
In July, Russia employed a different AI-enabled drone in combat that demonstrated a less comprehensive form of autonomous targeting
The strike, on a gas station in Zaporizhzhia, killed three Ukrainian civilians
Human operators selected the gas station as the target area, while onboard software independently picked the final aim point
Russia is also integrating versions of a similar technology into its Geran series unmanned aerial vehicles, which are based on Iran’s delta-wing Shaheed-136 attack drone
Some Gerans include a seeker guidance package that allows the onboard computer to guide the drone in the final flight phase, after a human operator initially selects the target
Ukraine, for its part, has focused on modular AI-driven packages , including chips with embedded software and sometimes cameras, that it can install widely across drone and other platforms
It has fielded drones that use onboard AI to identify targets and guide them in their final flight phase
One such module tracks targets and guides the drone the final 500 meters to them
The company that makes the computer advertises more advanced modules, which it claims will provide additional and even full autonomy
Ukraine claims to have used more advanced autonomous drones on the battlefield as well

Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said in July that Ukraine used a drone that autonomously chooses targets with no radio connection to a human pilot in strikes in Russian-occupied Crimea at an unspecified date
He added that Ukraine has not mass-produced this drone
Ukraine also reportedly employed what have been dubbed fully autonomous quadcopter drones two years ago against Russian forces near Bakhmut, Ukraine, killing Russian soldiers
However, reports that the drones were preprogrammed raise questions about whether the drones independently selected the targets
Smoke rises from Russian oil producer Gazprom Neft’s Moscow oil refinery on Sept. 20, 2026, after a drone attack

AFP via Getty Images Battlefield advantages, ethical concerns Russian and Ukrainian drones with autonomous capabilities already have had battlefield impact, even though Kyiv and Moscow have not yet deployed the most advanced systems in large numbers
Drones with autonomous functions reduce their dependence on communications links and can continue despite jamming and other forms of electronic warfare
