<title>Lula’s UN address points to two starkly different visions of Brazilian nationalism ahead of crucial election</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761538/original/file-20260922-50-p6t6te.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C80%2C4280%2C2853&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">President of Brazil Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/president%C2%A0of-brazil%C2%A0luiz-in%C3%A1cio-lula-da-silva-speaks-during-news-photo/2296573897?adppopup=true"> Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>When Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva addressed the United Nations General Assembly on Sept. 22, 2026, the Brazilian president posed a question to both an international and domestic audience: Who is to decide Brazil’s future?</p>

<p>It is an unusually pressing question this year. Voters in Latin America’s largest nation head to the polls on Oct. 4, marking the culmination of a campaign defined by a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/sep/01/us-trump-rubio-meddling-brazil-election">greater degree of U.S. interference</a> than any election in recent memory. Although President Donald Trump has established a <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c8r8gxjxz10o">surprising personal rapport</a> with the left-wing elder statesman, the U.S. administration doesn’t hide its preference for Flávio Bolsonaro. He is the son of the disgraced former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently <a href="https://apnews.com/article/jair-bolsonaro-sentence-coup-home-bf37e7ee479349cb9c7a00339e984a83">serving a lengthy sentence</a> after being convicted of attempting to overturn the results of the 2022 election. </p>

<p>Lula has responded to U.S. pressure – which has included tariffs, sanction threats and revoked visas – by <a href="https://responsiblestatecraft.org/trump-brazil-tariffs/">making sovereignty</a> a central theme of his campaign, arguing that Brazil’s political destiny must be set by Brazilians rather than what he sees as a capricious foreign power.</p>

<p>Lula’s language has been uncompromising and often colorful. At a campaign rally outside the capital, Brasília, on Sept. 16, Lula <a href="https://g1.globo.com/politica/noticia/2026/09/16/lula-critica-eduardo-e-flavio-bolsonaro-de-dia-mostra-a-bandeira-nacional-e-de-noite-vai-ficar-de-quatro-para-os-estados-unidos.ghtml">declared Brazil</a> would not tolerate politicians who “by day display the national flag and at night get on all fours for the United States.” </p>

<p>He has <a href="https://www.congressoemfoco.com.br/noticia/120202/lula-chama-familia-bolsonaro-de-traidora-da-patria-por-atuar-nos-eua">denounced members</a> of the Bolsonaro family as traitors conspiring against the national interest in pursuit of personal gain. Such rhetoric has contributed to Lula’s <a href="https://www.reuters.com/3fec1b0a85a0/world/americas/brazils-lula-would-beat-bolsonaro-by-1-point-runoff-suggests-btgnexus-poll-2026-09-21/">small but steady lead</a> in most polls. </p>

<p>The underlying argument predates the current confrontation with Washington — and it’s also older than Lula himself, who would be sworn in at the age of 81 should he prevail in the national vote. Nationalism today might be “the master concept of the radical right,” <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfordhb/9780190274559.013.2">as one scholar of extremism has put it</a>, but it has never belonged exclusively to reactionaries in Brazil. </p>

<h2>Dueling notions of the nation</h2>

<p>As I document in my new book, “<a href="https://www.ucpress.edu/books/claiming-the-nation/hardcover">Claiming the Nation</a>,” Brazilian political movements both left and right throughout the 20th century competed to claim the nationalist mantle. In so doing, they argued about who was best positioned to ensure the nation lived up to its extraordinary natural potential while ascribing very different meanings to concepts like sovereignty and the national interest.</p>

<p>One of these political traditions – which can broadly be grouped as progressive nationalist – understood national sovereignty as the capacity to determine Brazil’s economic and political development on its own terms. For its proponents, a country could not be fully independent while its resources and institutions remained excessively dependent on decisions made elsewhere.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Throngs of demonstrators march with flags and a large effigy." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761297/original/file-20260921-50-p19u41.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761297/original/file-20260921-50-p19u41.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761297/original/file-20260921-50-p19u41.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761297/original/file-20260921-50-p19u41.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761297/original/file-20260921-50-p19u41.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761297/original/file-20260921-50-p19u41.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761297/original/file-20260921-50-p19u41.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Supporters of Flávio Bolsonaro march with an effigy of U.S. President Donald Trump holding a doll depicting Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva as a prisoner.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/The%20top%20photos%20of%20the%20week%20by%20AP%20photojournalists/b899b4abce0b4b1ab59c4be62de40418/photo">AP Photo/Andre Penner</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>A more conservative opposing strain of nationalism emerged after World War II in response to Brazil’s first era of mass democratic politics and presented Brazil’s failures less as a consequence of foreign dependence than of its own populist political class. This tradition viewed progressive nationalism as using promises of reform and demagogic tirades against scapegoats abroad to distract from their own corruption and irresponsibility. </p>

<p>These two nationalist traditions offered starkly different diagnoses of Brazil’s problems and divergent political prescriptions.</p>

<p>While Lula’s current appeals to sovereignty belong to the progressive tradition, they should not be mistaken for anti-Americanism. Brazil’s progressive nationalists have <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/20027635.pdf%20and%20https://www.jstor.org/stable/20455000?seq=1">historically sought</a> greater room for maneuver in the international system precisely because they understood national autonomy to depend on the ability to engage the world without becoming subordinate to any single power. </p>

<p>In that vein, Brazil has cultivated relations across ideological divides while seeking a larger voice in shaping the international order. Its efforts to assert that role, whether by pursuing a permanent seat on the U.N. Security Council or offering to mediate seemingly intractable geopolitical disputes, have <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/world-latin-america-65307553">often been dismissed</a> as <a href="https://www.foreignaffairs.com/brazil/what-happened-lula">naive or misguided</a>. As one <a href="https://www.project-syndicate.org/commentary/why-lula-consorting-with-putin-and-maduro-by-andres-velasco-2023-08">commentator put it</a>: “To behave as though Brazil could wield global power comparable to China’s, or even India’s, is pure folly.” </p>

<p>Yet such dismissals overlook the foreign-policy ambitions of a large and complex nation that has historically aspired to an important global role. Sovereignty, in this formulation, is less a demand for withdrawal than a claim to political agency. </p>

<h2>The Bolsonaro reaction</h2>

<p>Flávio Bolsonaro, by contrast, criticizes Brazilian democratic institutions – particularly the <a href="https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/flavio-bolsonaro-gathers-thousands-to-denounce-moraes-dictatorship-and-criticize-lula/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX09XRUZWQzU1MDIxMzM0MjE3MDAx">Supreme Court</a> and the <a href="https://valorinternational.globo.com/politics/news/2026/07/22/flavio-bolsonaro-repeats-debunked-voting-claims-to-ambassadors.ghtml">electoral system</a> – as obstacles to restoring the country’s political order. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A man waves his hands in the air toward supporters." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761302/original/file-20260921-50-e4wv61.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761302/original/file-20260921-50-e4wv61.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761302/original/file-20260921-50-e4wv61.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761302/original/file-20260921-50-e4wv61.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761302/original/file-20260921-50-e4wv61.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761302/original/file-20260921-50-e4wv61.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761302/original/file-20260921-50-e4wv61.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Flávio Bolsonaro rides on a man’s shoulders during his campaign rally at the site where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, was injured by a stabbing attack in 2018.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Trump%20fans%20in%20Brazil%2C%20Rubio%20honored%2C%20and%20other%20top%20photos%20from%20Latin%20America%20and%20the%20Caribbean/c3e78f8054dd45ca885ce971f2bf83f1/photo">AP Photo/Bruna Prado</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>From this perspective, a closer relationship with the U.S. is perfectly compatible with national renewal. If sovereignty for Lula means defending Brazil’s freedom to chart its own course in the world, for Bolsonaristas it means reclaiming Brazil from the domestic forces he and his supporters blame for its decline. </p>

<p>Flávio Bolsonaro’s main target is the judiciary that prosecuted and ultimately imprisoned his father. His <a href="https://www.infomoney.com.br/politica/flavio-diz-que-buscara-anistia-para-bolsonaro-ainda-durante-governo-de-transicao/">promise to free</a> Jair Bolsonaro is presented not as a rejection of the rule of law but as part of a broader pledge to reform institutions that, in his telling, have exceeded their proper authority. </p>

<p>The irony is that, notwithstanding his nationalist posturing, a Flávio Bolsonaro electoral victory would strengthen the transnational far-right current that many critics see Trump as embodying, extending the reach of a political project deeply hostile to popular sovereignty abroad.</p>

<h2>Brasília by way of New York</h2>

<p>In his U.N. speech, Lula insisted that powerful countries cannot dictate the political choices of weaker ones. That message comes weeks after a leaked <a href="https://www1.folha.uol.com.br/colunas/monicabergamo/2026/09/abin-alerta-governo-e-tse-sobre-nivel-critico-de-escalada-de-pressao-dos-eua-contra-o-brasil-nas-eleicoes.shtml">confidential report</a> from Brazil’s national intelligence service described the U.S. pressure campaign as having reached a “critical” level.</p>

<p>Shared with the Justice Ministry and the Superior Electoral Court, Brazil’s supreme body on elections, the report indicates that, for the first time in decades, foreign influence has become serious enough to warrant the attention of the institutions charged with protecting Brazil’s political and electoral system.</p>

<p>The U.N. was an ideal stage for Lula because it allows Brazil to reassert the principles of its independent foreign policy without signaling a retreat from international engagement. </p>

<p>That sovereignty argument has paid political dividends at home. But the campaign has increasingly been pulled back toward another elemental fault line in Brazilian politics: corruption. The <a href="https://theconversation.com/banking-scandal-rocks-brazils-politics-and-the-countrys-presidential-election-in-october-291931">crisis surrounding Banco Master</a>, a failed financial institution whose owner is at the center of a sprawling investigation into fraud, money laundering and political influence, has pushed the issue to the forefront of the campaign. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A demonstrator in a costume holds two flags." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761299/original/file-20260921-50-4nw5hn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761299/original/file-20260921-50-4nw5hn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761299/original/file-20260921-50-4nw5hn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761299/original/file-20260921-50-4nw5hn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761299/original/file-20260921-50-4nw5hn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761299/original/file-20260921-50-4nw5hn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761299/original/file-20260921-50-4nw5hn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A Bolsonaro supporter wears a costume with Brazilian and U.S. flag motifs at a Brazilian Independence Day event on Sept. 7, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Brazil%20Independence%20Day/b09edb3ecd13404ab05cb6888fd16451/photo">AP Photo/Andre Penner</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Ironically, while Lula is not directly implicated <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/brazilian-top-court-unseals-probe-into-multibillion-dollar-bank-fraud-2026-09-11/">in the scandal</a> and Flávio Bolsonaro <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/may/14/flavio-bolsonaro-banker-film-jair-bolsonaro">very much is</a>, the incumbent seems to be the one paying a political price for one of the largest financial scandals in Brazilian history. The more the campaign turns from sovereignty to corruption, the more vulnerable Lula becomes.</p>

<p>Nor is Lula enjoying the traditional polling bump that incumbents have <a href="https://www.nexojornal.com.br/story/lula-pesquisa-atlasintel-efeito-incumbencia">historically received</a> late in the campaign. Despite relatively robust job growth and low inflation over Lula’s third term, the cost of living has been a central campaign issue dogging the president. The economy might be slowing down at exactly the wrong time for Lula’s electoral chances. </p>

<p>Security is another top-of-mind issue that favors the challenger, <a href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/brazilian-voters-latest-eye-bukele-052451783.html">who has promised an approach</a> modeled after El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele.</p>

<h2>The pre-election lines in the sand</h2>

<p>For generations, Brazilian politicians have argued over whether the country’s frustrations are best explained by forces beyond its borders or by failures within them. Washington has hardly been a neutral observer. </p>

<p>Throughout much of the 20th century, Washington <a href="https://cebri.org/revista/en/artigo/237/brazil-and-the-united-states-on-a-collision-course">often quietly</a> intervened <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/blar.12518">to shape the political choices</a> available to Brazilian governments, most <a href="https://nsarchive2.gwu.edu/NSAEBB/NSAEBB118/index.htm">notably in its support</a> for the 1964 coup. </p>

<p>What is unique about this election, however, is that the U.S. is taking sides so openly and in real time through <a href="https://www.wola.org/analysis/brazil-united-states-relations-election/">hostile policy measures</a> designed to put a thumb on the scale of the country’s political debate. Sovereignty, once invoked to debate development, economic dependence and Brazil’s place in the international order, has become an immediate question of de facto political authority. </p>

<p>Flávio Bolsonaro does not reject national sovereignty. Instead, he locates threats to that sovereignty primarily inside Brazil, in institutions and political actors he regards as having thwarted his family’s political agenda. </p>

<p>Lula very pointedly locates the threat differently, emphasizing the ability to resist a foreign power’s undue exertions of leverage. They represent competing answers to the older question of what is needed for Brazil to remain master of its own destiny.</p>

<p>On Oct. 4, Brazilians will determine which understanding of the national interest will guide their nation in an increasingly uncertain global order. The choice is whether Brazil’s sovereignty means charting its own course or accepting one charted, at least in part, somewhere else.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290470/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: President of Brazil Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly

Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images When Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva addressed the United Nations General Assembly on Sept. 22, 2026, the Brazilian president posed a question to both an international and domestic audience: Who is to decide Brazil’s future? It is an unusually pressing question this year
Voters in Latin America’s largest nation head to the polls on Oct. 4, marking the culmination of a campaign defined by a greater degree of U.S. interference than any election in recent memory
Although President Donald Trump has established a surprising personal rapport with the left-wing elder statesman, the U.S. administration doesn’t hide its preference for Flávio Bolsonaro
He is the son of the disgraced former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently serving a lengthy sentence after being convicted of attempting to overturn the results of the 2022 election

Lula has responded to U.S. pressure – which has included tariffs, sanction threats and revoked visas – by making sovereignty a central theme of his campaign, arguing that Brazil’s political destiny must be set by Brazilians rather than what he sees as a capricious foreign power
Lula’s language has been uncompromising and often colorful

At a campaign rally outside the capital, Brasília, on Sept. 16, Lula declared Brazil would not tolerate politicians who “by day display the national flag and at night get on all fours for the United States.” He has denounced members of the Bolsonaro family as traitors conspiring against the national interest in pursuit of personal gain
Such rhetoric has contributed to Lula’s small but steady lead in most polls
The underlying argument predates the current confrontation with Washington — and it’s also older than Lula himself, who would be sworn in at the age of 81 should he prevail in the national vote
Nationalism today might be “the master concept of the radical right,” as one scholar of extremism has put it , but it has never belonged exclusively to reactionaries in Brazil

Dueling notions of the nation As I document in my new book, “ Claiming the Nation ,” Brazilian political movements both left and right throughout the 20th century competed to claim the nationalist mantle

In so doing, they argued about who was best positioned to ensure the nation lived up to its extraordinary natural potential while ascribing very different meanings to concepts like sovereignty and the national interest

One of these political traditions – which can broadly be grouped as progressive nationalist – understood national sovereignty as the capacity to determine Brazil’s economic and political development on its own terms
For its proponents, a country could not be fully independent while its resources and institutions remained excessively dependent on decisions made elsewhere
Supporters of Flávio Bolsonaro march with an effigy of U.S
President Donald Trump holding a doll depicting Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva as a prisoner

AP Photo/Andre Penner A more conservative opposing strain of nationalism emerged after World War II in response to Brazil’s first era of mass democratic politics and presented Brazil’s failures less as a consequence of foreign dependence than of its own populist political class
This tradition viewed progressive nationalism as using promises of reform and demagogic tirades against scapegoats abroad to distract from their own corruption and irresponsibility
These two nationalist traditions offered starkly different diagnoses of Brazil’s problems and divergent political prescriptions
While Lula’s current appeals to sovereignty belong to the progressive tradition, they should not be mistaken for anti-Americanism

Brazil’s progressive nationalists have historically sought greater room for maneuver in the international system precisely because they understood national autonomy to depend on the ability to engage the world without becoming subordinate to any single power
In that vein, Brazil has cultivated relations across ideological divides while seeking a larger voice in shaping the international order
Its efforts to assert that role, whether by pursuing a permanent seat on the U.N
Security Council or offering to mediate seemingly intractable geopolitical disputes, have often been dismissed as naive or misguided

As one commentator put it : “To behave as though Brazil could wield global power comparable to China’s, or even India’s, is pure folly.” Yet such dismissals overlook the foreign-policy ambitions of a large and complex nation that has historically aspired to an important global role
Sovereignty, in this formulation, is less a demand for withdrawal than a claim to political agency

The Bolsonaro reaction Flávio Bolsonaro, by contrast, criticizes Brazilian democratic institutions – particularly the Supreme Court and the electoral system – as obstacles to restoring the country’s political order
Flávio Bolsonaro rides on a man’s shoulders during his campaign rally at the site where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, was injured by a stabbing attack in 2018
AP Photo/Bruna Prado From this perspective, a closer relationship with the U.S. is perfectly compatible with national renewal

If sovereignty for Lula means defending Brazil’s freedom to chart its own course in the world, for Bolsonaristas it means reclaiming Brazil from the domestic forces he and his supporters blame for its decline
Flávio Bolsonaro’s main target is the judiciary that prosecuted and ultimately imprisoned his father
His promise to free Jair Bolsonaro is presented not as a rejection of the rule of law but as part of a broader pledge to reform institutions that, in his telling, have exceeded their proper authority

The irony is that, notwithstanding his nationalist posturing, a Flávio Bolsonaro electoral victory would strengthen the transnational far-right current that many critics see Trump as embodying, extending the reach of a political project deeply hostile to popular sovereignty abroad
Brasília by way of New York In his U.N. speech, Lula insisted that powerful countries cannot dictate the political choices of weaker ones
That message comes weeks after a leaked confidential report from Brazil’s national intelligence service described the U.S. pressure campaign as having reached a “critical” level

Shared with the Justice Ministry and the Superior Electoral Court, Brazil’s supreme body on elections, the report indicates that, for the first time in decades, foreign influence has become serious enough to warrant the attention of the institutions charged with protecting Brazil’s political and electoral system
The U.N. was an ideal stage for Lula because it allows Brazil to reassert the principles of its independent foreign policy without signaling a retreat from international engagement
That sovereignty argument has paid political dividends at home
But the campaign has increasingly been pulled back toward another elemental fault line in Brazilian politics: corruption

title: When your child asks if they’ll be harmed like the people on the news, what do you say? Psychologists provide tips on how to talk about identity

<title>When your child asks if they’ll be harmed like the people on the news, what do you say? Psychologists provide tips on how to talk about identity</title>
    <content type="html"><p>Imagine your child asks you out of the blue, “If we speak Spanish, will they take you away?” Or imagine them suddenly asking what an offensive slur means. When a child asks these types of questions, it can be difficult to trace them back to a specific news story or event. But you may not need to. The question itself tells you that your child is trying to make sense of something they heard.</p>

<p>As parents, we’ve each had some version of these conversations with our young children.</p>

<p>The fear takes different forms in different families. For some children, it’s a question about whether their family may be harmed because of the language they speak. For others, it may be about their skin color, gender, religion or the person they love. Underneath is often the same concern that <a href="https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2018/10/generation-z-stressed">young people across the country</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10578-020-00972-z">are grappling with</a>: What do these messages mean for people like me?</p>

<p>Children whose identities aren’t directly targeted are listening too. <a href="https://theconversation.com/american-society-teaches-everyone-to-be-racist-but-you-can-rewrite-subconscious-stereotypes-141676">Public discourse teaches children</a> which differences are treated as ordinary, which are treated as suspect and who is allowed to belong <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8721.2007.00496.x">without having to explain themselves</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=w8MYwHYAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">As psychologists</a> <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=erJnbxwAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">who study</a> and treat <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/a0034733">anxiety</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpr.2016.04.001">depression</a> as well as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/23794925.2022.2025630">research resilience</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/15332640.2025.2467191">among diverse groups</a> of children and families, we frequently hear versions of this question in our work and at our kitchen tables.</p>

<p>Parents cannot control every message their child encounters, but they can help their child understand what those messages do and do not mean.</p>

<h2>Listen for the sideways question</h2>

<p>Parents often imagine that an important conversation will announce itself clearly: “Something I heard on the news made me worried about being Latina.” </p>

<p>Usually, it doesn’t. A younger child may ask whether a classmate’s family is safe or whether something that happened to someone else could happen to them too. An older child may repeat something they saw online, make a joke or suddenly go quiet when a topic related to identity comes up.</p>

<p>Children often <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00444">don’t have the vocabulary</a> to name a fear directly or the confidence that a topic is safe to raise. We’ve seen this pattern again and again when we work with families in the clinic: Teasing a fear out by going sideways, such as through someone else’s situation or a hypothetical, can allow a child to gauge how an adult will react before deciding whether to ask their real question.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760365/original/file-20260916-60-haanio.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Father kneeling down holding hand of child outside" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760365/original/file-20260916-60-haanio.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760365/original/file-20260916-60-haanio.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760365/original/file-20260916-60-haanio.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760365/original/file-20260916-60-haanio.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760365/original/file-20260916-60-haanio.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760365/original/file-20260916-60-haanio.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760365/original/file-20260916-60-haanio.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Some children need assurance before they can ask a hard question.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/father-holding-hands-with-son-royalty-free-image/527168866">Ed Bock/The Image Bank via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In our experience, younger children sometimes find it easier to talk about a worry through a drawing, a stuffed animal or a story about “a kid who felt scared about something” rather than addressing it head-on. If a direct question stalls out, shifting the format – rather than repeating the question – can help children open up.</p>

<p>Instead of immediately correcting or reassuring your child, get curious first. Research on <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chiabu.2007.03.021">how children respond to different kinds of questions</a> has consistently found that open-ended prompts like “tell me more” draw out far more than direct or yes or no questions. That principle can be useful at the dinner table too: “What made you think about that?” may get further than “Are you scared about something?”</p>

<p>If a child says “I don’t know,” resist the urge to press further in that moment. Not knowing yet is a normal response; sometimes kids may <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s42761-021-00040-2">need more time</a> to make sense of a feeling before they can put words to it. You can leave the door open instead: “That’s OK. If you think of it later, I’m here.” This tells your child the invitation still stands without turning it into an interrogation.</p>

<h2>Don’t leave the meaning blank</h2>

<p>Parents sometimes avoid talking about difficult news because they don’t want to frighten their children. But if a child has heard people like them described as dangerous, defective, unwanted or less worthy, changing the subject doesn’t erase the message. Neither does staying silent. It simply leaves children to work out on their own what that message means about them.</p>

<p>Instead of changing the subject, minimizing what they heard or saying “don’t worry about it,” parents can answer directly: “Some people believe that, but we don’t.” They can tell their child directly that comments that demean someone because of who they are aren’t acceptable.</p>

<p>Research on <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/0012-1649.42.5.747">ethnic-racial socialization</a> – that is, the ways parents teach children about race and ethnicity – suggests that messages about cultural history, traditions and pride can be just as important for children’s self-esteem and sense of identity as conversations that prepare them for prejudice. </p>

<p>Studies on LGBTQ+ youth show a similar pattern: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1744-6171.2010.00246.x">Greater family acceptance during adolescence</a> is associated with higher self-esteem and better health, as well as lower rates of depression, substance use and <a href="https://theconversation.com/trans-youth-are-significantly-more-likely-to-attempt-suicide-when-gender-dysphoria-is-met-with-conversion-therapy-than-with-hormone-treatment-207592">suicidal thoughts</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760363/original/file-20260916-50-hmus7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Parent smiling down at child leaning head against their arm while seated in a restaurant" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760363/original/file-20260916-50-hmus7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760363/original/file-20260916-50-hmus7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760363/original/file-20260916-50-hmus7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760363/original/file-20260916-50-hmus7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760363/original/file-20260916-50-hmus7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760363/original/file-20260916-50-hmus7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760363/original/file-20260916-50-hmus7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Affirming that you love and respect your child no matter their identity can protect their well-being.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/mom-and-daughter-waiting-for-food-in-hotel-kid-in-royalty-free-image/2150982295">Raja J/iStock via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Parents can reassure their child that there is nothing wrong with being autistic or that they don’t need to be afraid of people who pray differently from them. They can confirm that they and their family belong – in this home, community and country – regardless of what anyone else says.</p>

<p>The goal isn’t to pretend discrimination doesn’t exist. It’s to help children – whether they are the ones being targeted or are watching it happen to someone else – separate what people say about an identity from what that identity actually means about a person’s worth.</p>

<p>Children deserve explicitly positive messages from trusted adults. Even when those  messages seem obvious or your child already knows them, saying them out loud anyway could help reinforce that their worth was never actually in question. It can also give children something to hold onto when they encounter hurtful messages in the future.</p>

<h2>Don’t wait for a crisis to talk about identity</h2>

<p>Silence itself can take a toll. Research has linked <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10802-023-01133-1">avoiding conversations about ongoing threats</a> to worse mental health in children during times of crisis.</p>

<p>Making identity an ordinary part of family life can help children experience it as a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/0012-1649.42.5.747">source of pride</a> rather than only a subject of conflict. Families can talk casually about culture and history, and challenge stereotypes when they encounter them. They can present difference as natural instead of as a tragedy or include people of different identities in everyday conversations.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760366/original/file-20260916-50-zbcshx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Parent and child talking over two bowls of food." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760366/original/file-20260916-50-zbcshx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760366/original/file-20260916-50-zbcshx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760366/original/file-20260916-50-zbcshx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760366/original/file-20260916-50-zbcshx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760366/original/file-20260916-50-zbcshx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760366/original/file-20260916-50-zbcshx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760366/original/file-20260916-50-zbcshx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">When identity is a regular topic of conversation, it can be easier to approach difficult questions about it later on.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/mother-and-daughter-having-breakfast-in-kitchen-royalty-free-image/2262549563">Miljan Živković/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>These conversations don’t need to start with a big, formal sit-down, and starting small may actually work better. Research suggests the <a href="https://hechingerreport.org/too-few-parents-talk-to-their-kids-about-race-and-identity-report-finds/">earlier and more casually</a> these topics about identity come up, the more normal they become. This could look like pointing out a character’s different skin tone in a board book, or noticing aloud why a toy aisle is divided by color. Waiting for a “big talk” can actually make the topic feel heavier than it needs to.</p>

<p>The message is simple: This part of you did not become unworthy of love, respect or belonging because someone attacked it. It was worthy before the headline appeared.</p>

<h2>Come back to the conversation</h2>

<p>Whereas adults may be able to more quickly move on with their daily lives after feeling disturbed or frightened by upsetting media, children may experience <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fped.2016.00026">more elevated and prolonged stress</a>.</p>

<p>A child who heard someone on the news describe people like those in their family as a threat in May may still be carrying that message in August. Studies that followed <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/a0034703">African American adolescents</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/15313204.2024.2420647">Latino/a adolescents</a> have found a link between experiences of discrimination and depressive symptoms that linger years later.</p>

<p>So come back to the conversation. Let a week or two pass, and then follow up with your child. For example: “Remember when you told me about the comment you heard that made your stomach feel yucky? Have you thought about it or had that yucky feeling again?”  </p>

<p>Your child may say they haven’t thought about it. Nonetheless, research suggests that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.13908">repeated conversations that promote pride</a> in a young person’s identity can protect them against ongoing racial discrimination. One study found that for LGBTQ+ youth who often experience <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/cou0000556">frequent and ongoing stress and discrimination</a> related to their identity, continuous explicit affirmation from their parents can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1744-6171.2010.00246.x">serve as a powerful buffer</a>: “I will always love and support you and make sure you get the respect that you deserve.”</p>

<h2>Why parents should speak now</h2>

<p>Often, the question a child is actually asking, underneath the silence, the joke or the shrugged-off comment is simple: Am I OK? Is there something wrong with people like me?</p>

<p>The majority of children in the U.S. are <a href="https://www.census.gov/newsroom/blogs/random-samplings/2023/05/racial-ethnic-diversity-adults-children.html">children of color</a>, <a href="https://mapresearch.org/policy-and-issue-analysis/LGBTQ-youth/">LGBTQ+</a> or <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/autism/data-research/index.html">neurodivergent</a>, or they live in households with at least one <a href="https://cmsny.org/publications/2024-mass-deportation-program-devastate-american-families-101024/">undocumented family member</a>.</p>

<p>These children are growing up in a world where parts of who they are are debated, stigmatized or portrayed as problems in public discourse, and the <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-to-protect-your-family-from-horrific-news-images-and-still-stay-informed-181818">news is not background noise</a>. They may encounter stories about <a href="https://theconversation.com/federal-immigration-enforcement-near-schools-disrupts-attendance-traumatizes-students-and-damages-their-academic-performance-273325">immigration raids</a> and <a href="https://theconversation.com/there-are-long-lasting-negative-effects-for-children-like-liam-ramos-who-are-detained-or-watch-their-parents-be-deported-274271">deportation threats</a>; <a href="https://theconversation.com/anti-trans-bills-and-political-climates-are-taking-a-significant-mental-health-toll-on-trans-and-nonbinary-people-even-during-pride-199859">anti-trans political advertising</a>; violence targeting people <a href="https://theconversation.com/when-us-fights-in-the-middle-east-american-muslim-students-often-face-discrimination-277676">because of their race or religion</a>; commentary portraying <a href="https://theconversation.com/no-evidence-links-autism-with-terrorism-but-ill-judged-statements-and-headlines-will-lead-to-stigma-164133">autism</a>, <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-neurodivergent-people-really-think-about-the-words-used-to-describe-them-271784">dyslexia</a> or <a href="https://theconversation.com/think-therapy-is-navel-gazing-think-again-173312">mental health care</a> in demeaning or misleading ways. </p>

<p>Across these stories, children may hear the same underlying question: Are people like me accepted and valued, or are we considered a problem?</p>

<p>Research has linked racial and ethnic discrimination and identity-related stigma to a wide <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/amp0000204">range of negative outcomes in adolescence</a>, including depression, poor self-esteem and declines in academic engagement. A 2023 report from The Trevor Project, a nonprofit focusing on suicide prevention among LGBTQ+ youth, documented that 86% of transgender and nonbinary youth said public debates over anti-trans bills had <a href="https://www.thetrevorproject.org/blog/new-poll-emphasizes-negative-impacts-of-anti-lgbtq-policies-on-lgbtq-youth/">negatively affected their mental health</a>. </p>

<p>The point isn’t that every identity or every form of discrimination works the same way. But parents giving consistent messages of “you are worthy and you belong” to their children can help them heal.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>When our own children express fears that who they are may put their family in danger, we don’t have a perfect answer ready. What we tell them, more or less, is that they heard some scary and untrue things, and that who we are and where we come from are things we never need to be ashamed of. It’s not the last time we’ll talk about it, and that’s the point.</p>

<p>Parents cannot create a world where their children never encounter prejudice or misinformation about who they are. But they can help their children make sense of what they heard, separate <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-do-people-hate-people-224252">someone else’s hate</a> from their self-worth and return to the conversation after everyone else has moved on.</p>

<p>So speak now. And continue to speak. Not because the news reminded you to, but because your child will be listening.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290768/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Imagine your child asks you out of the blue, “If we speak Spanish, will they take you away?” Or imagine them suddenly asking what an offensive slur means
When a child asks these types of questions, it can be difficult to trace them back to a specific news story or event
The question itself tells you that your child is trying to make sense of something they heard
As parents, we’ve each had some version of these conversations with our young children
The fear takes different forms in different families
For some children, it’s a question about whether their family may be harmed because of the language they speak
For others, it may be about their skin color, gender, religion or the person they love

Underneath is often the same concern that young people across the country are grappling with : What do these messages mean for people like me? Children whose identities aren’t directly targeted are listening too
Public discourse teaches children which differences are treated as ordinary, which are treated as suspect and who is allowed to belong without having to explain themselves

As psychologists who study and treat anxiety and depression as well as research resilience among diverse groups of children and families, we frequently hear versions of this question in our work and at our kitchen tables
Parents cannot control every message their child encounters, but they can help their child understand what those messages do and do not mean

Listen for the sideways question Parents often imagine that an important conversation will announce itself clearly: “Something I heard on the news made me worried about being Latina.” Usually, it doesn’t
A younger child may ask whether a classmate’s family is safe or whether something that happened to someone else could happen to them too
An older child may repeat something they saw online, make a joke or suddenly go quiet when a topic related to identity comes up
Children often don’t have the vocabulary to name a fear directly or the confidence that a topic is safe to raise

We’ve seen this pattern again and again when we work with families in the clinic: Teasing a fear out by going sideways, such as through someone else’s situation or a hypothetical, can allow a child to gauge how an adult will react before deciding whether to ask their real question
Some children need assurance before they can ask a hard question

Ed Bock/The Image Bank via Getty Images In our experience, younger children sometimes find it easier to talk about a worry through a drawing, a stuffed animal or a story about “a kid who felt scared about something” rather than addressing it head-on
If a direct question stalls out, shifting the format – rather than repeating the question – can help children open up
Instead of immediately correcting or reassuring your child, get curious first
Research on how children respond to different kinds of questions has consistently found that open-ended prompts like “tell me more” draw out far more than direct or yes or no questions

That principle can be useful at the dinner table too: “What made you think about that?” may get further than “Are you scared about something?” If a child says “I don’t know,” resist the urge to press further in that moment
Not knowing yet is a normal response; sometimes kids may need more time to make sense of a feeling before they can put words to it
You can leave the door open instead: “That’s OK
If you think of it later, I’m here.” This tells your child the invitation still stands without turning it into an interrogation
Don’t leave the meaning blank Parents sometimes avoid talking about difficult news because they don’t want to frighten their children
But if a child has heard people like them described as dangerous, defective, unwanted or less worthy, changing the subject doesn’t erase the message
It simply leaves children to work out on their own what that message means about them

Instead of changing the subject, minimizing what they heard or saying “don’t worry about it,” parents can answer directly: “Some people believe that, but we don’t.” They can tell their child directly that comments that demean someone because of who they are aren’t acceptable

Research on ethnic-racial socialization – that is, the ways parents teach children about race and ethnicity – suggests that messages about cultural history, traditions and pride can be just as important for children’s self-esteem and sense of identity as conversations that prepare them for prejudice

Studies on LGBTQ+ youth show a similar pattern: Greater family acceptance during adolescence is associated with higher self-esteem and better health, as well as lower rates of depression, substance use and suicidal thoughts
Affirming that you love and respect your child no matter their identity can protect their well-being
Raja J/iStock via Getty Images Parents can reassure their child that there is nothing wrong with being autistic or that they don’t need to be afraid of people who pray differently from them
They can confirm that they and their family belong – in this home, community and country – regardless of what anyone else says
The goal isn’t to pretend discrimination doesn’t exist

It’s to help children – whether they are the ones being targeted or are watching it happen to someone else – separate what people say about an identity from what that identity actually means about a person’s worth
Children deserve explicitly positive messages from trusted adults
Even when those messages seem obvious or your child already knows them, saying them out loud anyway could help reinforce that their worth was never actually in question
It can also give children something to hold onto when they encounter hurtful messages in the future
Don’t wait for a crisis to talk about identity Silence itself can take a toll

<title>The SAT has changed since it debuted 100 years ago – but questions remain about its relevance</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760871/original/file-20260918-50-urj9x7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C5%2C4688%2C3125&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">More than 2 million students took the SAT exam in 2025. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/multiple-choice-royalty-free-image/871734396?phrase=sat%20test&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true"> zimmytws/iStock/Getty Images Plus </a></span></figcaption></figure><p>In June 1926, the SAT exam was first administered to 8,000 high school students who hoped <a href="https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/pages/frontline/shows/sats/where/timeline.html">to attend elite universities</a>. </p>

<p>The SAT has undergone many changes <a href="https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED562579.pdf">since its original form 100 years ago</a>, ranging from how the test is administrated to what kinds of subject matter it covers. </p>

<p>One particularly big shift came around 2000, when about 280 colleges and universities <a href="https://www.insidehighered.com/admissions/article/2019/04/01/more-colleges-go-test-optional-admissions">allowed applicants to apply</a> without submitting scores for the SAT or the ACT, another common standardized test. Today, <a href="https://www.insidehighered.com/news/admissions/traditional-age/2026/08/28/90-colleges-dont-require-test-scores-2026-27">approximately 86% of colleges</a> and universities are test-optional. </p>

<p>Whether <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/answer-sheet/wp/2014/04/22/what-does-the-sat-measure-aptitude-achievement-anything/">the SAT accurately measures students’ academic strengths continues to be debated</a>. Some research shows that the test offers a strong indication of students’ <a href="https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/sat-student-success-stem.pdf">skills, knowledge and potential for college success</a>. </p>

<p>Other research points to fundamental flaws of SAT and ACT testing, including that <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2019/10/03/rich-students-get-better-sat-scores-heres-why.html">students from higher-income families tend to have higher SAT scores</a>. The test, after all, costs money to take, and wealthier families can afford tutors and prep classes. Wealthier students also typically attend well-funded public or private high schools. </p>

<p>As <a href="https://sites.mst.edu/bethkaniagosche/">a professor of education</a>, I think that understanding the history of the SAT is helpful to understanding the current debate surrounding it.  </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=SAT%20exam&amp;mediaType=photo">Alex Brandon/Associated Press</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>A new kind of exam</h2>

<p>The <a href="https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/pages/frontline/shows/sats/where/timeline.html">SAT was developed in the 1920s</a> by the College Board, an organization founded in 1900 by the presidents of 12 leading universities to standardize the college admissions process.</p>

<p>At the time, each university had its own variation of entrance exam. These tests were in essay format and written and graded by professors. </p>

<p>In 1926, a uniform SAT exam was <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/06/11/for-the-100th-anniversary-of-the-sat-a-look-at-standardized-test-scores-over-time/?utm_source=chatgpt.com">used for the first time</a>. It had 315 questions, with a time limit of 97 minutes. This gave test-takers about 18 seconds to answer each question – though students were not expected to answer every single question.</p>

<p>The original exam <a href="https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED562571.pdf">included nine sections</a>, some similar to those that students would see today, like paragraph reading and arithmetic. But other sections, like <a href="https://cognitivemetrics.com/test/1926-SAT">artificial language</a>, are no longer in use. Artificial language meant writing coded sentences using a set of complicated rules such as “<a href="https://cognitivemetrics.com/test/1926-SAT/AL">plurals are formed by adding -o</a>.”</p>

<p>In 1928 and 1929, as well as from 1936-1941, the SAT had no math questions. In 1930-1935, the math questions were <a href="https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED562579.pdf">all free response, rather than multiple choice</a>, as is standard today. </p>

<p>At the time, the SAT was revolutionary because it was not an essay exam with subjects and questions chosen by one university’s professors. </p>

<p>Multiple choice or fill-in-the-blank exam questions could be quickly and objectively scored. High school students no longer had to travel to a college campus to take an entrance exam. The SAT allowed thousands of students to take the same exam closer to home, removing the barrier of travel to campus. </p>

<p>The scores were viewed by multiple colleges, rather than just the one. This meant the SAT created both more competition and access to college.</p>

<p>But not all colleges or even high school teachers embraced the idea, in part because of concerns about a test dictating high school curricula.</p>

<p>The SAT was still used relatively rarely around this time, with about <a href="https://freshairarchive.org/segments/history-standardized-test">10,000 students sitting for the exam</a> each year in the late 1930s <a href="https://www.edweek.org/teaching-learning/made-to-measure/1999/06">and early 1940s</a>.</p>

<p>In 1947, Educational Testing Services, <a href="https://www.ets.org/Media/Research/pdf/Nonprofit.pdf">a private nonprofit organization devoted to testing and educational research</a>, was created to administer the SAT and develop other exams. This organization had an incentive to sell the SAT to institutions, resulting in more widespread use. </p>

<h2>The SAT gains traction</h2>

<p>Starting after World War II, universities experienced a <a href="https://www.ets.org/Media/Research/pdf/Nonprofit.pdf">sharp increase in college applicants who benefited from the GI Bill</a>. This <a href="https://www.va.gov/education/about-gi-bill-benefits/">government program offered educational</a> and financial assistance to military veterans. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/document-deep-dive-what-was-on-the-first-sat-21720496/?itm_source=related-content&amp;itm_medium=parsely-api">Universities began to strengthen their admissions criteria</a> and rely more on the SAT to weed out some applicants. </p>

<p>The University of California system became the <a href="https://www.highereddive.com/news/why-some-colleges-arent-reviewing-sat-and-act-scores/580558/">first and largest public system to require the SAT</a> in 1960. This was also the year that the <a href="https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/100-years-ago-students-across-the-us-took-the-first-sat-today-relatively-few-colleges-require-the-test-where-is-it-headed-180988997/">ACT was created</a>. </p>

<p>Over the next few decades, more schools began requiring the SAT as part of the standard admissions process. </p>

<p>In an effort to prevent students from relying too much on private tutors, the <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/how-the-sat-has-changed-over-the-past-90-years-2019-8#1960s-1970s-the-rise-of-the-test-prep-industry-and-the-controversy-surrounding-coaching-3">test creators also expanded the length of the exam and revised the questions</a>. </p>

<p>In <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/06/11/for-the-100th-anniversary-of-the-sat-a-look-at-standardized-test-scores-over-time/">1994, another change occurred when students used physical calculators</a> on the SAT for the first time. </p>

<h2>Not just a test</h2>

<p>Taking the SAT or the ACT is a high-stakes moment for students. Not only is their college admission potentially riding on the score, but a small score increase of 50-100 points could also mean thousands of dollars in scholarships. </p>

<p>The achievement gap between different racial groups on SAT scores <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/sat-math-scores-mirror-and-maintain-racial-inequity/">has been both well documented</a> and debated for decades.</p>

<p>Asian students have the highest average score for any ethnic group, <a href="https://nces.ed.gov/fastfacts/display.asp?id=171">followed by white students</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2026/07/a-century-of-the-sat/">Wealthier students are 13 times more likely</a> than low-income students to score a 1300 or higher on the SAT, out of a maximum 1,600 points. </p>

<p>Some research shows a link between <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/the-complex-ramifications-of-students-for-fair-admissions-v-harvard/">family income and students’ test scores</a> and college success, as defined as GPA, retention and graduation. </p>

<p>Other research indicates that a student’s <a href="https://www.nber.org/papers/w34975">high school GPA</a> is a better predictor of college success than SAT scores. </p>

<h2>Colleges and universities reconsider the SAT</h2>

<p>Because of concerns about the usefulness of the SAT in college admissions, around 2000 about 280 colleges and universities moved to make the SAT an <a href="https://fairtest.org/test-optional/">optional part of the admissions process</a>.</p>

<p>The start of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 served as a natural experiment for test-optional admissions. Students simply could not sit to <a href="https://newsroom.collegeboard.org/college-board-cancels-may-sat-response-coronavirus">take the SAT</a> due to virus transmission concerns, so almost no universities required either the SAT or ACT for admission in 2020 or 2021. </p>

<p>Six years later, over 2,000 colleges and universities <a href="https://fairtest.org/test-optional-list/">are still</a> test-optional – although the <a href="https://www.insidehighered.com/opinion/views/2024/01/22/what-does-test-optional-really-mean-opinion">categorization may be deceiving</a>, as some scholarships may depend on SAT scores. </p>

<p>More than 2 million students, or <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/education/2026/01/18/standardized-test-popularity/">approximately 47% of graduating high school</a> students, <a href="https://newsroom.collegeboard.org/sat-participation-class-2025-surpasses-2-million-test-takers-first-time-2020">took the SAT in 2025</a> – marking the highest number since before the pandemic.</p>

<p>And 36%, or 1.38 million, took the ACT that year.</p>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/rachel-barr-17-of-scarborough-takes-a-pre-sat-test-in-a-news-photo/512448684?adppopup=true">Shawn Patrick Ouellette/Portland Press Herald via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>

<h2>A high school ritual</h2>

<p>The SAT continues to be modified. </p>

<p>In 2024, it was shortened from three hours to <a href="https://allaccess.collegeboard.org/sat-still-measures-what-matters">two hours and 15 minutes</a>. The shortened time is closer to the original exam from 100 years ago, <a href="https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2026/07/a-century-of-the-sat/">which lasted 97 minutes.</a>. </p>

<p>Also in 2024, the SAT <a href="https://newsroom.collegeboard.org/digital-sat-launches-across-country-completing-transition-digital-and-providing-simpler-testing">went fully digital</a>. </p>

<p>The exam isn’t a perfect reflection of students’ potential and skills, but it continues to be the rite of passage that most high school students undertake as they look ahead to college.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/287551/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

As a professor of education , I think that understanding the history of the SAT is helpful to understanding the current debate surrounding it
The COVID-19 pandemic offered an experiment for universities that hadn’t already made the SAT optional for applicants

Alex Brandon/Associated Press A new kind of exam The SAT was developed in the 1920s by the College Board, an organization founded in 1900 by the presidents of 12 leading universities to standardize the college admissions process
At the time, each university had its own variation of entrance exam
These tests were in essay format and written and graded by professors
In 1926, a uniform SAT exam was used for the first time
It had 315 questions, with a time limit of 97 minutes
This gave test-takers about 18 seconds to answer each question – though students were not expected to answer every single question
The original exam included nine sections , some similar to those that students would see today, like paragraph reading and arithmetic
But other sections, like artificial language , are no longer in use

Artificial language meant writing coded sentences using a set of complicated rules such as “ plurals are formed by adding -o .” In 1928 and 1929, as well as from 1936-1941, the SAT had no math questions
In 1930-1935, the math questions were all free response, rather than multiple choice , as is standard today
At the time, the SAT was revolutionary because it was not an essay exam with subjects and questions chosen by one university’s professors
Multiple choice or fill-in-the-blank exam questions could be quickly and objectively scored
High school students no longer had to travel to a college campus to take an entrance exam
The SAT allowed thousands of students to take the same exam closer to home, removing the barrier of travel to campus
The scores were viewed by multiple colleges, rather than just the one
This meant the SAT created both more competition and access to college
But not all colleges or even high school teachers embraced the idea, in part because of concerns about a test dictating high school curricula
The SAT was still used relatively rarely around this time, with about 10,000 students sitting for the exam each year in the late 1930s and early 1940s
In 1947, Educational Testing Services, a private nonprofit organization devoted to testing and educational research , was created to administer the SAT and develop other exams
This organization had an incentive to sell the SAT to institutions, resulting in more widespread use
The SAT gains traction Starting after World War II, universities experienced a sharp increase in college applicants who benefited from the GI Bill
This government program offered educational and financial assistance to military veterans
Universities began to strengthen their admissions criteria and rely more on the SAT to weed out some applicants
The University of California system became the first and largest public system to require the SAT in 1960
This was also the year that the ACT was created
Over the next few decades, more schools began requiring the SAT as part of the standard admissions process
In an effort to prevent students from relying too much on private tutors, the test creators also expanded the length of the exam and revised the questions
In 1994, another change occurred when students used physical calculators on the SAT for the first time
Not just a test Taking the SAT or the ACT is a high-stakes moment for students

title: It’s OK if managers step in to help their sales staff – but not too much
url:
<title>It’s OK if managers step in to help their sales staff – but not too much</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761126/original/file-20260921-50-fz1udz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7008%2C4672&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Shoppers can take cues when managers step in to help their staff.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://unsplash.com/photos/a-couple-of-people-standing-in-front-of-a-fruit-stand-glr2gjR-9Yw">Grab on Unsplash</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Workers in sales might roll their eyes when they deal with a micromanaging boss. But many customers actually appreciate it if a store manager offers to help when they’re mulling over a purchase, whether it’s a dishwasher, a tablet or a lawnmower.</p>

<p>That’s the main finding of a new study I co-authored.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=3kiUy3QAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">scholar of sales and pricing</a>, I <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/00222429261448212">delved into this question</a>, along with fellow researchers <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=vkgxHEwAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">Molly R. Burchett</a> and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ZlTaK80AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">Brian Murtha</a>, by analyzing data from a massive field study involving more than 5.5 million real-world exchanges at a Fortune 500 company, in addition to six related experiments.</p>

<p>We found that this kind of intervention does pay off – to a certain extent. Sales teams that included a manager outperformed teams without one by 5% to 13%, which meant an extra US$13 million in yearly revenue at the company in question. The biggest lift came when a manager joined a sales teams dealing with new customers – and assumed a supportive role rather than taking a lead.</p>

<p>We were somewhat surprised by the lift from managers taking a back-seat role, so we ran some additional experiments. We found that customers view this kind of secondary support positively in that it boosted the status of the salesperson and team. This perception, in turn, increased their openness to buy, and ultimately increased sales. </p>

<h2>Why it matters</h2>

<p>It’s fairly common for managers to step in this way. <a href="https://careertrainer.ai/en/reports/sales-coaching-effectiveness-statistics/">Between 12%</a> and <a href="https://www.peerlab.ai/blog/what-sales-managers-actually-do-all-week/">20% of all sales managers</a> will help an associate close a sale, according to prior research. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/00222429261448212">In our survey</a> of 85 business-to-consumer managers, they reported a somewhat higher share, noting that they spend 41% of their time with their salespeople selling.</p>

<p>Sectors where this is especially common include <a href="https://capitaloneshopping.com/research/online-clothing-shopping-statistics">clothing and accessories</a> as well as <a href="https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/reports/files/Harvard_JCHS_Improving_Americas_Housing_2025_Embargoed.pdf">home improvement</a>.</p>

<p>More generally, managers have to juggle different demands at once. And to be effective, they have to know how to best allocate time across managerial tasks and interaction with customers. Some believe that a sales manager’s main job is to <a href="https://store.hbr.org/product/sales-managers-must-manage/64309?srsltid=AU7gw4X3DzsaS1z550aAClEWPh2CqQTT1az_bMAYcyQkFC6zdISIEkL7">manage, not sell</a>; others believe managers should be deeply <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/08853134.2023.2257391">involved in the sales process</a>. </p>

<p>Given these disparate approaches, we wanted to conduct research that might provide a decision framework to help managers allocate their time more effectively.</p>

<h2>What still isn’t known</h2>

<p>This research is only an initial foray into understanding managers and sales. For example, our findings don’t offer guidance on business-to-business sales, which are more complex. In those cases, buyers and sellers are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1509/jmkg.71.3.001">much more informed</a> about the goods or services in question, and much more <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0022242919899381">information is transferred</a>.</p>

<p>It’s possible that the impact of manager involvement in these settings may depend on the stage of the process. It’s also possible that managers should sometimes take the front seat rather than the back seat at different stages of business-to-business sales.</p>

<h2>What other research is being done</h2>

<p>There’s a sizable body of research on sales managers that tends to focus on their <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11747-017-0557-2">leadership behaviors</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/peps.12123">coaching</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jretai.2008.09.006">role-modeling</a>. This stream of literature, broadly speaking, suggests that managers have a big impact on sales performance, and that these soft skills are worth developing – even though they take time and effort to cultivate.</p>

<p>Up to this point, however, research on sales managers’ selling role remains limited. </p>

<h2>What’s next</h2>

<p>Our research focused on immediate, transaction-level outcomes of manager involvement in sales teams. Future work could seek to understand other results, like finding out exactly when this type of interference from above becomes counterproductive, or what the long-term effects of managers taking more of a hands-on role with sales might be.</p>

<p>We already have some initial hints on store-level performance and salesperson turnover. Manager involvement in individual sales improves store sales to a certain point, by around one of every three transactions. Beyond that range, store sales suffer, maybe because managers can’t perform their other duties. </p>

<p>As for turnover, we find that new salespeople who experience 10% more manager involvement in their first month are 8% less likely to quit by the third month than their counterparts. </p>

<p>We plan to continue this research to see which of these initial insights hold.</p>

<p><em>The <a href="https://theconversation.com/us/topics/research-brief-83231">Research Brief</a> is a short take on interesting academic work.</em></p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291745/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
